results.name: two_digit_example_multiple_contrast
results.description: Among targets >=10 from every example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of some example >=13 but of no example 2-12, minus yes-rate for targets that are not multiples, divisors or gcd>=3 kin of any example; observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route still over-credits multiples of large two-digit examples (a times-table effect), observed > null means it under-credits them.
results.code:
# name: two_digit_example_multiple_contrast
# description: Among targets >=10 from every example and sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of some example >=13 but of no example 2-12, minus yes-rate for targets that are not multiples, divisors or gcd>=3 kin of any example; observed < null means the model's size-independent multiples route still over-credits multiples of large two-digit examples (a times-table effect), observed > null means it under-credits them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    mult = (pres & (e1 > 1) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    divi = (pres & (np.mod(e1, t) == 0) & (t != e)).any(1)
    g = np.gcd(t.astype(int), e1.astype(int))
    kin = (pres & (g >= 3)).any(1)
    small = pres & (e1 >= 2) & (e1 <= 12) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)
    large = pres & (e1 >= 13) & (np.mod(t, e1) == 0) & (t != e)
    base = (d >= 10) & ~digmatch
    return diff(base & large.any(1) & ~small.any(1), base & ~mult & ~divi & ~kin)

results.name: gcd3_divisibility_contrast
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples whose greatest common divisor is exactly 3, yes-rate for multiple-of-3 targets minus non-multiples of 3, both restricted to targets sharing no example's final digit and not equal to an example; observed < null means people use 'multiple of 3' much more weakly than the model's single divisor penalty (shared with strict gcd-10 sets) implies, observed > null means more strongly.
results.code:
# name: gcd3_divisibility_contrast
# description: In sets of 2+ examples whose greatest common divisor is exactly 3, yes-rate for multiple-of-3 targets minus non-multiples of 3, both restricted to targets sharing no example's final digit and not equal to an example; observed < null means people use 'multiple of 3' much more weakly than the model's single divisor penalty (shared with strict gcd-10 sets) implies, observed > null means more strongly.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    ei = np.where(pres, ex, 0).astype(int)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(ei, axis=1)
    s = (g == 3) & (n >= 2)
    isex = ((t == e) & pres).any(1)
    base = s & ~digmatch & ~isex
    m3 = np.mod(t1, 3) == 0
    return diff(base & m3, base & ~m3)

results.name: round_target_in_nonround_even_set
results.description: In sets whose examples are all even and none ends in 0 or 5, yes-rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate for other even targets sharing no example's final digit; observed < null means people actively disfavour round numbers when the set is not round (the model treats them as ordinary non-matching evens), observed > null means a general round-number bonus the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: round_target_in_nonround_even_set
# description: In sets whose examples are all even and none ends in 0 or 5, yes-rate for multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate for other even targets sharing no example's final digit; observed < null means people actively disfavour round numbers when the set is not round (the model treats them as ordinary non-matching evens), observed > null means a general round-number bonus the model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    alleven = (~pres | (np.mod(e1, 2) == 0)).all(1)
    no05 = ~((np.mod(e1, 5) == 0) & pres).any(1)
    s = alleven & no05
    rnd = np.mod(t1, 10) == 0
    ev = np.mod(t1, 2) == 0
    return diff(s & rnd, s & ev & ~rnd & ~digmatch)

results.name: target_100_vs_other_round
results.description: Over sets not containing the target, yes-rate for target 100 minus yes-rate for targets 10-90 that are multiples of 10; observed > null means people give 100 a special landmark/endpoint status beyond the model's generic round-number, magnitude and divisor similarity, observed < null means the model over-credits 100.
results.code:

# description: Over sets not containing the target, yes-rate for target 100 minus yes-rate for targets 10-90 that are multiples of 10; observed > null means people give 100 a special landmark/endpoint status beyond the model's generic round-number, magnitude and divisor similarity, observed < null means the model over-credits 100.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0

    isex = ((t == e) & pres).any(1)
    a = (t1 == 100) & ~isex
    b = (np.mod(t1, 10) == 0) & (t1 < 100) & ~isex
    return diff(a, b)

results.name: five_ending_after_zero_examples
results.description: In sets with at least one example ending in 0 and none ending in 5, yes-rate for targets ending in 5 minus yes-rate for targets ending in 1-4 or 6-9 that share no example's final digit; observed > null means people extend round examples to the half-round class (multiples of 5), which the model's 0-ending-only round route and digit dims miss.
results.code:
# name: five_ending_after_zero_examples
# description: In sets with at least one example ending in 0 and none ending in 5, yes-rate for targets ending in 5 minus yes-rate for targets ending in 1-4 or 6-9 that share no example's final digit; observed > null means people extend round examples to the half-round class (multiples of 5), which the model's 0-ending-only round route and digit dims miss.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    has0 = ((np.mod(e1, 10) == 0) & pres).any(1)
    has5 = ((np.mod(e1, 10) == 5) & pres).any(1)
    s = has0 & ~has5
    u = np.mod(t1, 10)
    return diff(s & (u == 5), s & (u != 5) & (u != 0) & ~digmatch)

results.name: parity_set_distance_slope
results.description: In sets of 3+ examples all of one parity but not all sharing a final digit, OLS slope of yes on distance-to-nearest-example (per 10 units) among same-parity targets sharing no example's final digit; observed > null (flatter) means people generalize a parity rule uniformly across the range, observed < null means a steeper magnitude gradient than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: parity_set_distance_slope
# description: In sets of 3+ examples all of one parity but not all sharing a final digit, OLS slope of yes on distance-to-nearest-example (per 10 units) among same-parity targets sharing no example's final digit; observed > null (flatter) means people generalize a parity rule uniformly across the range, observed < null means a steeper magnitude gradient than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    p0 = np.mod(e1[:, 0], 2)
    par = (~pres | (np.mod(e1, 2) == p0[:, None])).all(1) & (n >= 3)
    u0 = np.mod(e1[:, 0], 10)
    run = (~pres | (np.mod(e1, 10) == u0[:, None])).all(1)
    a = par & ~run & (np.mod(t1, 2) == p0) & ~digmatch
    if a.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = d[a] / 10.0
    y = r[a]
    vx = np.var(x)
    if vx <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.mean((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean())) / vx)

results.name: digit_run_far_match_gradient
results.description: In sets of 3+ examples all sharing one final digit, yes-rate for same-final-digit targets >=20 from the nearest example minus same-digit targets <=10 from it (non-examples only); observed > null (less negative) means people apply the digit rule regardless of distance, whereas the model's coincidence sharpening also sharpens magnitude and so over-penalizes far rule-matching targets.
results.code:
# name: digit_run_far_match_gradient
# description: In sets of 3+ examples all sharing one final digit, yes-rate for same-final-digit targets >=20 from the nearest example minus same-digit targets <=10 from it (non-examples only); observed > null (less negative) means people apply the digit rule regardless of distance, whereas the model's coincidence sharpening also sharpens magnitude and so over-penalizes far rule-matching targets.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    u0 = np.mod(e1[:, 0], 10)
    run = (~pres | (np.mod(e1, 10) == u0[:, None])).all(1) & (n >= 3)
    same = np.mod(t1, 10) == u0
    isex = ((t == e) & pres).any(1)
    base = run & same & ~isex
    return diff(base & (d >= 20), base & (d <= 10))

results.name: round_set_near_miss_rate
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all multiples of 10, yes-rate for non-multiple-of-10 targets within 10 of the nearest example; observed < null means people reject near-but-off-rule targets more strictly than the model's (sharpened) magnitude similarity allows, observed > null means the model is too strict.
results.code:
# name: round_set_near_miss_rate
# description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all multiples of 10, yes-rate for non-multiple-of-10 targets within 10 of the nearest example; observed < null means people reject near-but-off-rule targets more strictly than the model's (sharpened) magnitude similarity allows, observed > null means the model is too strict.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t1 = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = t1[:, None]
    pres = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = pres.sum(1)
    e = np.where(pres, ex, 1e9)
    e1 = np.where(pres, ex, 1.0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    d = np.abs(t - e).min(1)
    digmatch = ((np.mod(t, 10) == np.mod(e1, 10)) & pres).any(1)
    def diff(a, b):
        if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
            return 0.0
        return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
    allr = (~pres | (np.mod(e1, 10) == 0)).all(1) & (n >= 2)

        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean())
